content.title: NASA’s Artemis II lifts off, sending four astronauts toward the moon
content.text: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (WAFF) - Artemis II successfully lifts off on Wednesday, sending four astronauts toward the moon for the first time in over 50 years! Updates:5:35 p.m. CTAt 5:35 p.m., the Artemis II rocket sent four brave souls on a 10-day trip to fly by the moon!Check out the video of the rocket launching off: Artemis II successfully lifts off on Wednesday, April 1, 2026, with four astronauts on board, making history, from Florida’s Space Coast!5:00 p.m. CTIt is almost go time!We are just a few minutes away from launch, and that means we are just a few minutes away from watching history at the Kennedy Space Center.The Artemis II crew is in their final minutes on Earth before a 10-day mission, going farther than ever before.“We’ve got boosters, we’ve got core stage, we’ve got engines, we’ve got an upper stage, we’ve got adapters, but my team is the team that brings it all together,” said Brian Matisak, MSFC SLS Systems Engineering and Integration Manager. 4:40 p.m. CTNine people traveled up the elevator on the mobile launcher, and now the five members of the closeout crew will leave. The final four remain.Those four are the brave astronauts sitting on 730,000 gallons of fuel, ready to head around the moon.The launch window opens at 5:24 p.m. Central time and stays open for two hours on Wednesday in case of delay.At launch, it takes 8 million tons of thrust to get that rocket off the ground.4:30 p.m. CTWe are now less than an hour away from blast off! Thousands of people lined the beach to catch a glimpse of history.The Range issue is resolved, the hatch is now closed, and a lot is riding on this launch, literally and figuratively.Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch, and Canadian Astronaut Jeremy Hansen are in the last hour on Earth before flight, taking care of last-minute, must-do checks before liftoff.It took a lot of humans to develop the transportation for these astronauts to travel 280,000 miles away.3,800 suppliers across 49 states, to be exact.Those include small businesses that manufacture critical parts.4:00 p.m. CTThe issues with the Range have been resolved!3:50 p.m. CTIn just over an hour, the Artemis II rocket is expected to launch from Cape Canaveral, becoming the first manned mission to the moon in more than 50 years!The countdown clock continues, and everything is going smoothly with the rocket and the crew, but there is a problem on the Range.The Range is the flight path and airspace around the Kennedy Space Center.Right now, the Range is working on an issue with the SLS flight termination system, something that is only used if there is an emergency.This flight termination system is the self-destruct mechanism that would be used in case of an emergency. Artemis II missionThis is a mission designed to take humans farther into deep space and lay the groundwork for a return to the moon. The rocket will lift and push four astronauts into Low Earth Orbit to set them up for a trip around the moon for the first time in more than 54 years.This mission is a major step toward a continuing sequence of flights to the moon in the next few years, eventually building a moon base so humans can live and work there.All eyes are now on Wednesday’s launch window as the next era of space exploration gets underway.For the first time in more than 54 years, four astronauts will be taking that ride to space to make their moon landing!The point of this test flight is to let the pilots get a feel for the vehicle, practice “docking,” learn to make the transition from launch to living in the Crew vehicle for 10 days, test communications in deep space, take updated photos, and take us all along for the ride!Who’s on boardThe Space Launch System (SLS) is fueled up with more than 730,000 gallons of super-cooled propellant. A lot of people at the Kennedy Space Center and the Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) have been watching gauges, making sure that everything is going according to plan, especially after this rocket has experienced hydrogen leaks in the past few weeks. They are now going through the long checklist as they get ready for the afternoon launch.In the meantime, these four Artemis II astronauts have suited up in the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building. The four crew members got a weather briefing at around 11:30 a.m. Central time, and there is still about an 80 percent chance of good weather. The Crew Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch, a five-time space camper, and Canadian Astronaut Jeremy Hansen have had their lunch, and they’ve put on their Orion Crew Survival System flight suits. They were not even alive when the first Americans traveled around the moon. They are all between 47 and 50 years old.They committed to a first human mission that loops around the moon this century on a new deep space rocket, one that is much more advanced than the Saturn V.Each one of these four astronauts represents a first, too.Wiseman is a widower. His wife Carroll died of cancer six years ago, leaving him to raise his two teenage daughters. He is a Navy fighter pilot.Glover is a Naval aviator, too, and is the first Black astronaut to travel in deep space. He is married and has four children. Koch is married, is a Space Camp Hall of Famer, and she is the first female to travel in deep space after holding the record for the single longest spaceflight.Hansen is the first Canadian to travel in deep space. He is married with children and is a fighter pilot.The orange suits they are wearing are designed for launch, reentry, and emergency situations. These suits can sustain the crew for up to six days in an emergency.They’ve completed communication checks, leak checks, and mobility checks, and they’ve walked through the awaiting crowd of well-wishers to the launch pad to be hooked up inside the Orion. The Artemis II crew is now inside the Orion Crew Capsule, preparing for a history-making mission around the moon. The astronauts named the Orion Crew Capsule: Integrity.They are suited up, their helmets are on, and they are buckled in!Final preparations As of around 3 p.m. Central time, they are all doing their preflight checklist.Communication checks are underway between astronauts on the Artemis II rocket to Launch Control and Mission Control, which is vital so that lines of communication stay open at all times. North Alabama connectionsAround half a million people lined up at the beach in person to watch this history-making launch.That number is about the same as those who witnessed the Apollo 8 launch, which is the mission that Artemis II is mirroring.In 2026, the MSFC had an $8 billion economic impact on the state of Alabama, and supported 35,000 jobs, driven mostly by the Artemis program.$1.5 billion went to small businesses, and $3 billion in NASA funding went to big contracts.Alabama fingerprints are all over Artemis II!MSFC engineers designed and developed, and now manage the SLS program.More than 100 local companies in North Alabama contributed directly to the Artemis II mission, including contractors like Boeing and Teledyne-Brown Engineering, which made the Launch Vehicle Stage Adapter (LVSA) that connects the main rocket stage to the upper stage.United Launch Alliance in Decatur manufactured the Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage (ICPS), which provides propulsion to the Orion Crew Capsule.Then there is the RS-25 engine testing done by L3Harris, Northrop Grumman, and BK Aerospace, a company in rural Arab, which manufactured a side mount for a video camera that sits outside the SLS so NASA and the rest of us could watch Artemis II lift off. There are so many North Alabama hands on this rocket that once again will propel astronauts toward the moon and eventually build a permanent base there. Watch parties & Live updatesFor those who aren’t in Florida and want to share the excitement of this milestone flight, you can head to the huge launch party this afternoon at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center! Admission is free. This is a day like no other for these astronauts and for America’s space program!WAFF 48 will follow these astronauts and update as more information comes in during the next few hours before the launch, which is scheduled for 5:24 Central time on Wednesday afternoon. Live updates are also provided on NASA’s website throughout this historic day.
